body:
We looked at your PR during an ad-hoc GDScript team meeting. We still need to fully understand the workflow to properly assess your PR.

We discussed about the problem of "assuming" that `null` means not yet assigned. We were imagining maybe that we could fix this issue the same way we fixed cyclic dependencies, which is, on initialization, to create a placeholder script that would get updated afterwards by the content of the real script, but the reference being the same.

Let's talk about the whole problem in the #gdscript channel!

Thanks for your detailed description.

I noticed there is the function `ResourceLoaderText::recognize_script_class` which takes a resource file and returns its script class. If this could be made to work with scene files as well that would solve the whole issue. Then before instantiating the autoload scene we could create a dummy node with a dummy script attached which points to the correct script path, removing the problems during the analyze stage.

This would probably require adding the `script_class` tag to `gd_scene` scene files as well. If I were to implement the solution this way would it be likely to get merged? Or would it be too risky to add to the scene file format and we should prefer my current method?

Alternatively, I could also look for the script attached to the scene's root node without the `script_class` tag by parsing more than the first line of the file.

Rebased and slightly improved the code by not needlessly repeating a section. I have also investigated the viability of two alternative approaches:

**Using `ResourceLoaderText::recognize_script_class`**: As mentioned in my comment above, if there was a method that returned the script of a scene without needing to actually load the scene that would help this issue. Resources already have the `script_class` tag which could be utilized for scenes as well. However, this would only work for scripts that have a global `class_name` (unless the `script_class` tag were modified to also accept paths to scripts).

**Add the path to `AutoloadInfo`**. As was proposed in the last GDScript meeting, the path to the top-level script can be included with the rest of the autoload data inside `project.godot`. I tried it and it works, but one issue is that it still requires some way of retrieving the path to the top-level script of the scene when adding or modifying an autoload via the editor. This would require loading the entire scene every time the autoload setting is modified and would probably lead to noticeable lags.

My suggestion is therefore to check if my current solution might be fine as is. It is a bit of a "hack", but it touches very little code and doesn't modify the project settings or scene files of existing projects in any way and has none of the downsides mentioned above.

> My suggestion is therefore to check if my current solution might be fine as is. It is a bit of a "hack", but it touches very little code and doesn't modify the project settings or scene files of existing projects in any way and has none of the downsides mentioned above.

I'm not comfortable with introducing this hack, because the code lies at the edge of multiple pretty complex systems (autoloads, the resource loader and cache, the gdscript cache)

IMO we need to look into other options.

> **Add the path to `AutoloadInfo`**.

Looking at all the caching issue we had with the similar tech, used for `class_name` that might be hard to pull off :thinking:

> **Using `ResourceLoaderText::recognize_script_class`**

That's probably the best option we have at the moment. However we need to keep in mind that we also need to support binary resources. So basically a new method similar to `ResourceFormatLoader::get_resource_script_class`.

> However, this would only work for scripts that have a global `class_name`

That's a deal-breaker.

The way I'd go about it, is to not save anything new into the files. Instead we just start parsing the scene using `VariantParser` and stop as soon as reaching the initial node and looking at it's `script` property. Still a bit hacky, but at least somewhat self-contained.
